question.text: If $f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} \sin x + \sin 2x + \sin 3x & \sin 2x & \sin 3x \\ 3 + 4\sin x & 3 & 4\sin x \\ 1 + \sin x & \sin x & 1 \end{vmatrix}$, then $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} f(x)\,dx =$

solution.text:
Applying the column operation $C_1 \rightarrow C_1 - C_2 - C_3$, we get:

$f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} \sin x & \sin 2x & \sin 3x \\ 0 & 3 & 4\sin x \\ 0 & \sin x & 1 \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding the determinant along the first column:

$f(x) = \sin x (3 \times 1 - 4\sin x \times \sin x)$

$f(x) = \sin x (3 - 4\sin^2 x)$

$f(x) = 3\sin x - 4\sin^3 x = \sin 3x$

Now, evaluating the integral:

$\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} f(x)\,dx = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \sin 3x \,dx$

$= \left[ -\dfrac{\cos 3x}{3} \right]_{0}^{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}$

$= -\dfrac{1}{3} \left( \cos\left(\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) - \cos(0) \right)$

$= -\dfrac{1}{3} (0 - 1) = \dfrac{1}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{3}$

question.text: Let $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $pC_{11} + 4C_{21} - 5C_{32} = -2$, where $C_{ij}$ denotes the cofactor of an element $a_{ij}$ of matrix $A$, then the value of $p$ is :

solution.text:
Given matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$

The cofactor $C_{ij}$ is given by $(-1)^{i+j} M_{ij}$, where $M_{ij}$ is the minor of the element $a_{ij}$.

Calculating the required cofactors:

$C_{11} = (-1)^{1+1} \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = 1 \times (8 - 0) = 8$

$C_{21} = (-1)^{2+1} \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = -1 \times (4 - 2) = -2$

$C_{32} = (-1)^{3+2} \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -1 \times (0 - 2) = 2$

Substituting these values into the given equation $pC_{11} + 4C_{21} - 5C_{32} = -2$:

$p(8) + 4(-2) - 5(2) = -2$

$8p - 8 - 10 = -2$

$8p - 18 = -2$

$8p = 16$

$p = 2$

Answer: $2$

question.text: The lines $x+2 a y+a=0, x+3 b y+b=0, x+4 c y+c=0$ are concurrent then $a, \mathrm{~b}, \mathrm{c}$ are in

solution.text:
The condition for the given three lines to be concurrent is that the determinant of their coefficients must be zero.

$\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2a & a \\ 1 & 3b & b \\ 1 & 4c & c \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant along the first column:

$1(3bc - 4bc) - 1(2ac - 4ac) + 1(2ab - 3ab) = 0$

$-bc - (-2ac) + (-ab) = 0$

$2ac - bc - ab = 0$

$2ac = ab + bc$

Dividing the entire equation by $abc$:

$\dfrac{2ac}{abc} = \dfrac{ab}{abc} + \dfrac{bc}{abc}$

$\dfrac{2}{b} = \dfrac{1}{c} + \dfrac{1}{a}$

This implies that $\dfrac{1}{a}, \dfrac{1}{b}, \dfrac{1}{c}$ are in Arithmetic Progression.

Therefore, $a, b, c$ are in Harmonic Progression.

Answer: Harmonic progression

question.text:
If $A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\cos \theta & \sin \theta & 0 \\ -\sin \theta & \cos \theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right]$,
where $A_{21}, A_{22}, A_{23}$ are cofactors of $a_{21}, a_{22}, a_{23}$ respectively, then the value of $a_{21} A_{21}+a_{22} A_{22}+a_{23} A_{23}=$

solution.text:
The sum of the products of the elements of any row with their corresponding cofactors is equal to the determinant of the matrix.

Therefore, $a_{21} A_{21} + a_{22} A_{22} + a_{23} A_{23} = |A|$

Calculating the determinant of $A$:

$|A| = \cos \theta (\cos \theta \cdot 1 - 0) - \sin \theta (-\sin \theta \cdot 1 - 0) + 0$

$|A| = \cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1$

Thus, $a_{21} A_{21} + a_{22} A_{22} + a_{23} A_{23} = 1$

Answer: $1$

question.text: If \([2 \overline{\mathrm{p}}-3 \overline{\mathrm{r}} ~\overline{\mathrm{q}} ~\overline{\mathrm{s}}]+[3 \overline{\mathrm{p}}+2 \overline{\mathrm{q}} ~\overline{\mathrm{r}} ~\overline{\mathrm{s}}]=\mathrm{m}[\overline{\mathrm{p}} ~\overline{\mathrm{r}} ~\overline{\mathrm{s}}]+\mathrm{n}[\overline{\mathrm{q}} ~\overline{\mathrm{r}} ~\overline{\mathrm{s}}]+\mathrm{t}[\overline{\mathrm{p}} ~\overline{\mathrm{q}} ~\overline{\mathrm{s}}]\),, then the values of $m, n, t$ respectively are ....

solution.text:
Using the properties of scalar triple product:

$[2\bar{p} - 3\bar{r} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}] = [2\bar{p} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}] - [3\bar{r} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}]$

$= 2[\bar{p} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}] - 3[\bar{r} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}]$

Since $[\bar{r} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}] = -[\bar{q} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}]$, we get:

$[2\bar{p} - 3\bar{r} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}] = 2[\bar{p} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}] + 3[\bar{q} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}]$

Similarly, for the second term:

$[3\bar{p} + 2\bar{q} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}] = [3\bar{p} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}] + [2\bar{q} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}]$

$= 3[\bar{p} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}] + 2[\bar{q} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}]$

Adding the two expressions:

$[2\bar{p} - 3\bar{r} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}] + [3\bar{p} + 2\bar{q} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}] = 2[\bar{p} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}] + 3[\bar{q} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}] + 3[\bar{p} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}] + 2[\bar{q} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}]$

$= 3[\bar{p} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}] + 5[\bar{q} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}] + 2[\bar{p} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}]$

Comparing this with $m[\bar{p} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}] + n[\bar{q} \quad \bar{r} \quad \bar{s}] + t[\bar{p} \quad \bar{q} \quad \bar{s}]$, we get:

$m = 3$, $n = 5$, $t = 2$

Answer: $3,5,2$

question.text: If $w=\dfrac{-1-i \sqrt{3}}{2}$ where $i=\sqrt{-1}$, then the value of $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & w & w^2 \\ w & w^2 & 1 \\ w^2 & 1 & w\end{array}\right|$ is

solution.text:
Given $w = \dfrac{-1 - i\sqrt{3}}{2}$, which is a complex cube root of unity.

Therefore, $w^3 = 1$ and $1 + w + w^2 = 0$.

The given determinant is $\Delta = \left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & w & w^2 \\ w & w^2 & 1 \\ w^2 & 1 & w\end{array}\right|$.

Applying the column operation $C_1 \rightarrow C_1 + C_2 + C_3$, we get:

$\Delta = \left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 + w + w^2 & w & w^2 \\ 1 + w + w^2 & w^2 & 1 \\ 1 + w + w^2 & 1 & w\end{array}\right|$

Substituting $1 + w + w^2 = 0$:

$\Delta = \left|\begin{array}{ccc}0 & w & w^2 \\ 0 & w^2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & w\end{array}\right|$

Since all elements of the first column are zero, the value of the determinant is $0$.

Answer: 0

question.text: If the planes $ax = y + z$, $by = z + x$, $cz = x + y$ pass through a common line, then the value of $(a + b + c - abc) = \cdots$

solution.text:
The given equations of the planes can be rewritten as:

$ax - y - z = 0$
$-x + by - z = 0$
$-x - y + cz = 0$

Since the planes pass through a common line, the system of homogeneous equations has infinitely many solutions. Thus, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero.

$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} a & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & b & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & c \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant along the first row:

$a(bc - 1) - (-1)(-c - 1) + (-1)(1 + b) = 0$

$abc - a - c - 1 - 1 - b = 0$

$abc - a - b - c - 2 = 0$

$a + b + c - abc = -2$

Answer: $-2$

question.text: If $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 7 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$ then $\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} =$

solution.text:
The given matrix equation can be written as $x C_1 + y C_2 + z C_3 = B$, where $C_1, C_2, C_3$ are the columns of the coefficient matrix and $B$ is the constant matrix.

Substituting the given matrices:

$x \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} + y \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + z \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 7 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$

Notice that the constant matrix on the right side is identical to the third column of the coefficient matrix.

Comparing both sides, we get $x = 0$, $y = 0$, and $z = 1$.

Thus, $\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

Answer: $\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$

question.text: Let $A^T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, $B^T = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and $X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}$. If $AX = B$, then the values of $x, y, z$ are..........

solution.text:
Given $A^T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$, we have $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$.

Given $B^T = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, we have $B = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

The equation $AX = B$ can be written as:

$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$

This gives the system of equations:

$x + y + z = 6$

$x - y + 2z = 5$

$2x + y - z = 1$

Adding the first two equations gives:

$2x + 3z = 11$

Adding the second and third equations gives:

$3x + z = 6 \Rightarrow z = 6 - 3x$

Substituting $z$ into $2x + 3z = 11$ gives:

$2x + 3(6 - 3x) = 11$

$2x + 18 - 9x = 11$

$-7x = -7 \Rightarrow x = 1$

Substituting $x = 1$ into $z = 6 - 3x$ gives:

$z = 6 - 3(1) = 3$

Substituting $x = 1$ and $z = 3$ into $x + y + z = 6$ gives:

$1 + y + 3 = 6 \Rightarrow y = 2$

Thus, $x = 1, y = 2, z = 3$.

Answer: $x = 1, y = 2, z = 3$

question.text: If $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$ then the distance of point $P(a, b, c)$ from the plane $2x + y + 2z = 10$ is

solution.text:
The given matrix equation represents the following system of linear equations:

$2a + b - c = 4$

$-a + 2b + c = 0$

$a - b + 2c = -2$

Adding the first and second equations gives $a + 3b = 4$.

Adding the second and third equations gives $b + 3c = -2$.

Adding the first and third equations gives $3a + c = 2$.

Solving these equations, we get $a = 1$, $b = 1$, and $c = -1$.

The point $P(a, b, c)$ is $P(1, 1, -1)$.

The perpendicular distance of the point $P(1, 1, -1)$ from the plane $2x + y + 2z - 10 = 0$ is given by:

$d = \dfrac{|2(1) + 1(1) + 2(-1) - 10|}{\sqrt{2^2 + 1^2 + 2^2}}$

$d = \dfrac{|2 + 1 - 2 - 10|}{\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4}}$

$d = \dfrac{|-9|}{3} = 3$ units.

Answer: $3$ units.

question.text: If $\left[\begin{array}{lll}1 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 4\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l}12 \\ 15 \\ 13\end{array}\right]$, then the value of $x^2+y^2+z^2=$

solution.text:
The given matrix equation corresponds to the system of linear equations:

$x + 3y + 3z = 12$

$x + 4y + 4z = 15$

$x + 3y + 4z = 13$

Subtracting the first equation from the second equation:

$y + z = 3$

Subtracting the first equation from the third equation:

$z = 1$

Substituting $z = 1$ into $y + z = 3$:

$y + 1 = 3 \Rightarrow y = 2$

Substituting $y = 2$ and $z = 1$ into the first equation:

$x + 3(2) + 3(1) = 12 \Rightarrow x + 9 = 12 \Rightarrow x = 3$

The value of $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ is:

$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 3^2 + 2^2 + 1^2 = 9 + 4 + 1 = 14$

Answer: $14$

question.text: Let $A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right]$ and $B=\left[\begin{array}{l}4 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{array}\right]$ such that $\mathrm{AX}=\mathrm{B}$, then $\mathrm{X}=$

solution.text:
The given matrix equation $AX = B$ can be written as a system of linear equations:

$x - y + z = 4$

$2x + y - 3z = 0$

$x + y + z = 2$

Subtracting the third equation from the first equation gives:

$-2y = 2 \Rightarrow y = -1$

Substituting $y = -1$ into the first and second equations:

$x - (-1) + z = 4 \Rightarrow x + z = 3$

$2x + (-1) - 3z = 0 \Rightarrow 2x - 3z = 1$

Multiplying $x + z = 3$ by $3$ and adding to $2x - 3z = 1$ gives:

$3x + 3z + 2x - 3z = 9 + 1$

$5x = 10 \Rightarrow x = 2$

Substituting $x = 2$ into $x + z = 3$ gives:

$2 + z = 3 \Rightarrow z = 1$

Thus, $X = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.

Answer: $\left[\begin{array}{c}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{array}\right]$

question.text:
Let $X=\left[\begin{array}{l}\mathrm{a} \\ \mathrm{b} \\ \mathrm{c}\end{array}\right], \mathrm{A}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{array}\right]$ and $\mathrm{B}=\left[\begin{array}{l}3 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{array}\right]$.
If $A X=B$, then the value of $2 a-3 b+4 c$ will be

solution.text:
Given the matrix equation $AX = B$, we can write the system of linear equations as:

$a - b + 2c = 3$ ... (1)

$2a + c = 1$ ... (2)

$3a + 2b + c = 4$ ... (3)

From equation (2), we get $c = 1 - 2a$.

Substituting $c = 1 - 2a$ into equation (1):

$a - b + 2(1 - 2a) = 3$

$a - b + 2 - 4a = 3$

$-3a - b = 1 \Rightarrow b = -3a - 1$

Substituting $b = -3a - 1$ and $c = 1 - 2a$ into equation (3):

$3a + 2(-3a - 1) + (1 - 2a) = 4$

$3a - 6a - 2 + 1 - 2a = 4$

$-5a - 1 = 4$

$-5a = 5 \Rightarrow a = -1$

Now, substituting $a = -1$ back to find $b$ and $c$:

$b = -3(-1) - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2$

$c = 1 - 2(-1) = 1 + 2 = 3$

We need to find the value of $2a - 3b + 4c$:

$2a - 3b + 4c = 2(-1) - 3(2) + 4(3)$

$= -2 - 6 + 12$

$= 4$

Answer: 4

Now $|\mathrm{A}|=4+(-8)+9=5$
$$
\begin{aligned}
\therefore A^{-1} &=\left[\begin{array}{lll}

8 & -7 & 2 \\
9 & -6 & 1
\end{array}\right] \times \frac{1}{5} \\
\therefore\left[\begin{array}{l}
x \\
y \\
z

question.text: If $f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} x^2 & \sin x & e^x \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ p & p^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$ then $f''(0) = $

solution.text:
Given $f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} x^2 & \sin x & e^x \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ p & p^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$

Since the second and third rows are independent of $x$, we can differentiate the determinant by differentiating only the first row.

$f'(x) = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2) & \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x) & \dfrac{d}{dx}(e^x) \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ p & p^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 2x & \cos x & e^x \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ p & p^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$

Differentiating again with respect to $x$:

$f''(x) = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{d}{dx}(2x) & \dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x) & \dfrac{d}{dx}(e^x) \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ p & p^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -\sin x & e^x \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ p & p^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$

Substituting $x = 0$:

$f''(0) = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & -\sin 0 & e^0 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ p & p^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ p & p^2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$

Expanding the determinant along the first row:

$f''(0) = 2(1 - (-p^2)) - 0 + 1(2p^2 - p)$

$f''(0) = 2(1 + p^2) + 2p^2 - p$

$f''(0) = 4p^2 - p + 2$

Answer: $4p^2 - p + 2$

then the value of $a b c$ is

solution.text:
Since, $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}, \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}$, and $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}$ are non-coplanar vectors,
therefore $[\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}} \overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}] \neq 0$
$\Rightarrow \Delta=\left|\begin{array}{lll}1 & a & a^{2} \\ 1 & b & b^{2} \\ 1 & c & c^{2}\end{array}\right| \neq 0$
$\Rightarrow$
$\Delta \neq 0$
$$
\begin{array}{l}
\text { Now, } & \left(\begin{array}{lll}
